title: III. A Little Demon
paragraphs: Going in to Lise, he found her half reclining in the invalid chair in which she was wheeled about when she couldn't walk. She didn't move to meet him, but her sharp, keen eyes were riveted on his face. There was a feverish look in her eyes; her face was pale and yellow. Alyosha was astonished at the change that had come over her in three days. She was actually thinner. She didn't hold out her hand to him. He touched the thin, long fingers that lay motionless on her dress, then sat down facing her, without a word.
“I know you're in a hurry to get to the prison,” Lise said curtly, “and mamma's kept you for hours in there; she's just been telling you about me and Yulia.”
“How do you know?” Alyosha asked.
“I've been listening. Why do you stare at me? I wanted to listen, and I listened — there's no harm in that. I'm not going to apologize.”
“You're upset about something?”

“On the contrary, I'm very happy. Just now I was reflecting, for the thirtieth time, what a good thing it is I refused you and am not going to be your wife. You aren't fit to be a husband. If I were to marry you and give you a note to take to the man I loved after you, you'd take it and be sure to deliver it, and bring an answer back too. Even at forty, you'd still be carrying my love letters for me.”
She suddenly laughed.
“There's something spiteful about you and yet open-hearted,” Alyosha smiled at her.

“The open-heartedness is that I'm not ashamed of myself in front of you. What's more, I don't want to feel ashamed in front of you — in front of you above all. Alyosha, why is it I don't respect you? I'm very fond of you, but I don't respect you. If I respected you, I wouldn't talk to you without shame, would I?”
“No.”
“But do you believe that I'm not ashamed in front of you?”
“No, I don't believe it.”
Lise laughed nervously again; she spoke rapidly.
“I sent your brother, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, some sweets in prison. Alyosha, you know, you are rather pretty! I'll love you awfully for so quickly letting me off loving you.”
“Why did you send for me today, Lise?”
“I wanted to tell you a longing I have. I'd like someone to torment me — marry me and then torment me, deceive me and leave. I don't want to be happy.”
“You're in love with disorder?”

“Yes, I want disorder. I keep wanting to set the house on fire. I keep picturing how I'll creep up and set fire to the house on the sly — it must be on the sly. They'll try to put it out, but it'll go on burning. And I'll know and say nothing. Ah, what silliness! And how bored I am!”
She waved her hand with a look of disgust.
“It's your luxurious life,” Alyosha said softly.
“Is it better, then, to be poor?”
“Yes, it is better.”

“That's what your monk taught you. That's not true. Let me be rich and everyone else poor — I'll eat sweets and drink cream and not give any to anyone else. Ach, don't speak, don't say anything,” she waved her hand at him, though Alyosha hadn't opened his mouth. “You've told me all that before, I know it all by heart. It bores me. If I'm ever poor, I'll murder somebody, and even if I'm rich I may murder someone perhaps — why do nothing! But you know, I'd like to reap the harvest, to cut the rye? I'll marry you, and you'll become a peasant, a real peasant; we'll keep a colt — shall we? Do you know Kalganov?”
“Yes.”

“He's always wandering about, dreaming. He says, ‘Why live in real life? It's better to dream. You can dream the most delightful things, but real life is a bore.' But he'll be married soon for all that; he's already been making love to me. Can you spin tops?”
“Yes.”

“Well, he's just like a top: he wants to be wound up and set spinning, and then to be lashed, lashed, lashed with a whip. If I marry him, I'll keep him spinning all his life. You aren't ashamed to be with me?”
“No.”
“You're awfully cross because I don't talk about holy things. I don't want to be holy. What will they do to a person in the next world for the greatest sin? You must know all about that.”
“God will judge you,” Alyosha said, watching her steadily.

“That's just what I'd like. I'd go up and they'd judge me, and I'd burst out laughing in their faces. I'd dreadfully like to set fire to the house, Alyosha — to our house. You still don't believe me?”
“Why not? There are children of twelve who long to set fire to something, and do set things on fire too. It's a sort of disease.”
“That's not true, that's not true; there may be children, but that's not what I mean.”
“You take evil for good; it's a passing crisis, perhaps the result of your illness.”
“You do despise me, though! It's simply that I don't want to do good, I want to do evil, and illness has nothing to do with it.”
“Why do evil?”

“So that everything might be destroyed. Ah, how nice it would be if everything were destroyed! You know, Alyosha, I sometimes think of doing a fearful lot of harm, every bad thing I can, and I'd do it for a long time on the sly, and then suddenly everyone would find out. Everyone would stand around and point their fingers at me, and I'd look at them all. That would be awfully nice. Why would it be so nice, Alyosha?”
“I don't know. It's a craving to destroy something good — or, as you put it, to set fire to something. It happens sometimes.”
“I don't only say it, I will do it.”
“I believe you.”
“Ah, how I love you for saying you believe me. And you are not lying one little bit. But perhaps you think I'm saying all this on purpose to annoy you?”
“No, I don't think that ... though perhaps there's a little wish to do that in it too.”
“There is a little. I can never lie to you,” she declared, with a strange fire in her eyes.

What struck Alyosha above everything was her earnestness. There was not a trace of humor or jesting in her face now, though in the old days fun and gaiety had never deserted her, even at her most “earnest” moments.
“There are moments when people love crime,” said Alyosha thoughtfully.

“Yes, yes! You've uttered my own thought. They love crime — everyone loves crime — they love it always, not just at some ‘moments.' You know, it's as if people made an agreement to lie about it and have lied about it ever since. They all declare that they hate evil, but secretly they all love it.”
“And are you still reading nasty books?”
“Yes, I am. Mamma reads them and hides them under her pillow and I steal them.”
“Aren't you ashamed to destroy yourself?”

“I want to destroy myself. There's a boy here who lay down between the rails while the train was passing. Lucky fellow! Listen — your brother is being tried now for murdering his father, and everyone loves that he's killed his father.”
“Loves that he's killed his father?”
“Yes, loves it — everyone loves it! Everyone says it's so awful, but secretly they simply love it. I for one love it.”
“There's some truth in what you say about everyone,” Alyosha said softly.

“Oh, what ideas you have!” Lise shrieked in delight. “And you a monk, too! You wouldn't believe how I respect you, Alyosha, for never telling lies. Oh, I must tell you a funny dream of mine. I sometimes dream of devils. It's night; I'm in my room with a candle, and suddenly there are devils all over the place, in all the corners, under the table, and they open the doors — there's a crowd of them behind the doors, and they want to come in and seize me. And they're just coming in, just about to seize me. But I suddenly cross myself and they all draw back, though they don't go away altogether — they stand at the doors and in the corners, waiting. Then suddenly I have a frightful longing to revile God aloud, and so I begin, and then they come crowding back toward me, delighted, and seize me again — and I cross myself again and they all draw back. It's awful fun. It takes one's breath away.”
“I've had the same dream too,” Alyosha said suddenly.
“Really?” Lise cried, surprised. “I say, Alyosha, don't laugh, that's awfully important. Can two different people have the same dream?”
“It seems they can.”

“Alyosha, I tell you, it's awfully important,” Lise went on, with really excessive amazement. “It's not the dream that's important — it's your having had the same dream as me. You never lie to me — don't lie now: is it true? You're not laughing?”
“It's true.”
Lise seemed extraordinarily impressed, and for half a minute she was silent.
“Alyosha, come and see me, come and see me more often,” she said suddenly, in a pleading voice.
“I'll always come to see you, all my life,” Alyosha answered firmly.

“You're the only person I can talk to, you know,” Lise began again. “I talk to no one but myself and you. Only you in the whole world. And to you more readily than to myself. And I'm not a bit ashamed with you, not a bit. Alyosha, why am I not ashamed with you, not a bit? Alyosha, is it true that at Easter the Jews steal a child and kill it?”
“I don't know.”

“There's a book here in which I read about the trial of a Jew who took a child of four years old and cut off the fingers from both hands, and then crucified him on the wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him, and afterwards, when he was tried, he said the child died soon, within four hours. That was ‘soon'! He said the child moaned, kept on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That's nice!”
“Nice?”
“Nice. I sometimes imagine it was I who crucified him. He'd hang there moaning and I'd sit opposite him eating pineapple _compote_. I'm awfully fond of pineapple _compote_. Do you like it?”
Alyosha looked at her in silence. Her pale, sallow face was suddenly contorted, her eyes burned.

“You know, when I read about that Jew I shook with sobs all night. I kept picturing how the little thing cried and moaned (a child of four understands, you know), and all the while the thought of pineapple _compote_ haunted me. In the morning I wrote a letter to a certain person, begging him _particularly_ to come and see me. He came, and I suddenly told him all about the child and the pineapple _compote_. _All_ about it, _all_, and said it was nice. He laughed and said it really was nice. Then he got up and left. He was only here five minutes. Did he despise me? Did he despise me? Tell me, tell me, Alyosha, did he despise me or not?” She sat up on the couch, her eyes flashing.
“Tell me,” Alyosha asked anxiously, “did you send for that person?”
“Yes, I did.”
“Did you send him a letter?”
“Yes.”
“Simply to ask about that, about that child?”
“No, not about that at all. But when he came, I asked him about that at once. He answered, laughed, got up, and went away.”
“That person behaved honorably,” Alyosha murmured.
“And did he despise me? Did he laugh at me?”
“No, because perhaps he believes in the pineapple _compote_ himself. He's very ill now, too, Lise.”
“Yes, he does believe in it,” Lise said, with flashing eyes.
“He doesn't despise anyone,” Alyosha went on. “It's just that he doesn't believe anyone. And if he doesn't believe in people, of course he despises them.”
“Then he despises me, me?”
“You too.”
“Good,” Lise seemed to grind her teeth. “When he left laughing, I felt that it was nice to be despised. The child with its fingers cut off is nice, and to be despised is nice ...”
And she laughed in Alyosha's face, a feverish, malicious laugh.

“Do you know, Alyosha, do you know, I'd like — Alyosha, save me!” She suddenly jumped up from the couch, rushed to him, and seized him with both hands. “Save me!” she almost groaned. “Is there anyone in the world I could tell what I've told you? I've told you the truth, the truth. I'll kill myself, because I loathe everything! I don't want to live, because I loathe everything! I loathe everything, everything. Alyosha, why don't you love me in the least?” she finished in a frenzy.
“But I do love you!” Alyosha answered warmly.
“And will you weep over me — will you?”
“Yes.”
“Not because I won't be your wife, but simply weep for me?”
“Yes.”

“Thank you! It's only your tears I want. Everyone else can punish me and trample me underfoot, everyone, everyone, not excepting _any one_. Because I don't love anyone. Do you hear, not anyone! On the contrary, I hate him! Go, Alyosha — it's time you went to your brother.” She tore herself away from him suddenly.
“How can I leave you like this?” Alyosha said, almost in alarm.
“Go to your brother, the prison will be closing; go, here's your hat. Give my love to Mitya, go, go!”

And she almost forcibly pushed Alyosha out of the door. He looked at her in pained surprise, when he was suddenly aware of a letter in his right hand, a tiny letter folded up tight and sealed. He glanced at it and instantly read the address, “To Ivan Fyodorovitch Karamazov.” He looked quickly at Lise. Her face had become almost menacing.
“Give it to him, you must give it to him!” she ordered him, trembling and beside herself. “Today, at once, or I'll poison myself! That's why I sent for you.”

And she slammed the door quickly. The bolt clicked. Alyosha put the note in his pocket and went straight downstairs without going back to Madame Hohlakov — forgetting her, in fact. As soon as Alyosha had gone, Lise unbolted the door, opened it a little, slid her finger into the crack, and slammed the door with all her might, crushing her finger. Ten seconds later, freeing her finger, she walked softly, slowly, to her chair, sat up straight in it, and looked intently at her blackened finger and at the blood oozing from under the nail. Her lips were quivering and she kept whispering rapidly to herself:
“I'm a wretch, wretch, wretch, wretch!”
